sections.report:
**Walk (working notes).** The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on the serif headline, drops to the row of four illustrated cards, then goes to the dark "Book a visit" button at the top right. It reads as the landing page of a local home-services company: warm, tidy and friendly.

Job (assumed): a homeowner should understand what Fernway offers, roughly what it costs, and how to book.

The whole piece:
- One-sentence purpose: yes
- Main image and headline make one idea: yes (there is no hero image; the cards hold the illustrations)
- Every element does a job: yes
- One mood and era: yes
- Copy finished: yes
- Repeated elements consistent: yes
- Colors and shapes carry the mood: yes
- Headings name their sections: yes

Every line is yes, so step 5 has no entries to open.

---

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Two problems in the copy that this section has no line for. I'm passing them on for the director to file, probably under Text or as copy findings:
- **The laundry card contradicts the promise in the headline and subhead.** The headline says "on your schedule" and the subhead says "choose a day". The Laundry pickup card (about x 672–900, y 525–565) says "We collect on Monday and bring it back folded on Wednesday." A reader can take this two ways: pickup only happens on Mondays, or Monday to Wednesday is just an example. If it's the first, the page's main promise isn't true for this service and the customer finds out after they've counted on it. The fix is to say which it is, for example "Picked up the day you choose, back folded two days later." This is a defect: it's the kind of line a customer holds the company to. Weight: minor.
- **The prices have no unit.** "From $89 / $189 / $24 / $65" (y ≈ 614 on each card) don't say per what: a visit, a room, a bag of laundry, a lawn. "From $24" for laundry is especially open, since it could mean per load, per bag or per week. Without the unit, the viewer can't compare the services or budget for one, and the first price they're quoted may not match what they expected. The fix is to add the unit, for example "From $24 per bag". This is a defect, because it's a price the viewer acts on. Weight: minor, possibly major if pricing is what makes people book.

**What's working.**
- **It reads as one whole.** The warm cream background, the dark-teal serif wordmark and headline, a plain sans for the body, and flat illustrations in teal, coral and mustard all share one calm, domestic mood. That fits a service that sends strangers into your home, where trust matters.
- **The four cards follow one pattern exactly.** Each has the same pale-mint picture panel, a bold title, two lines of description and a teal "From $" price at the same baseline. The row scans as a comparison at a glance. The equal card height and fixed price position are worth keeping as copy lengths change.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
First read: the eye lands on the serif headline "Help around the house, on your schedule" (y≈115–200). It then drops to the row of four illustrated cards, which pull with roughly equal force, and picks up the dark "Book a visit" button at the top right. It reads as a local home-services landing page for homeowners, and it feels calm and friendly.

Job (assumed): a landing page that gets homeowners to pick a service and book.

Walk: What matters first
- One element dominates: **yes**. The headline is about 38 px bold serif, the largest and darkest type on the page. The four illustrations are big and bright, but they are split into four equal tiles and sit lower, so none of them beats it.
- Distinct levels below it: **yes**. Subhead about 17 px regular grey; card titles about 19 px bold near-black; card body about 15 px regular grey; prices about 15 px bold teal, set apart by weight and colour. The subhead (17 regular) and card titles (19 bold) are close in size but clearly separated by weight and value, and they sit in different places.
- Headings differ in more than size: **yes**. The headline is serif bold, the card titles are sans bold, and the body is sans regular grey.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly leads (about x56–675, y115–200).** It is bold serif, roughly twice the size of anything below it, and dark on cream. It is the only serif on the page apart from the logo, so the eye knows where to start even with four colourful illustrations below. Keep the cards' illustrations from growing or getting more saturated, or they will start to compete with it.
- **The levels inside each card are set apart by more than size.** Card titles are bold near-black, descriptions are regular grey, and prices are bold teal and pushed to the card's bottom edge (y≈614). Each card reads as name, then explanation, then cost, without needing a fourth type size.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. Bash was blocked, so I couldn't run the crop or entries scripts. At 1280×800 the image is one screen, so the crop script wouldn't have made crops anyway. I judged from the full image, and the findings below don't use the catalog entries.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** No. In each of the four cards the illustration panel starts about 14 px inside the card edge (card at x≈56, panel at x≈70). The title, description and price start about 20 px in (x≈76). The other cards repeat this, for example panel x≈368 and text x≈374 in card 2. The text therefore sits about 6 px to the right of the picture's left edge directly above it. That's too little to look intended and enough to show as a small step down the left side of every card. At the right edge the panel runs about 14 px from the card edge, while the text sits on a wider margin, so the picture also looks a little wider than the text column below it. The fix is to give the panel and the text the same inset so they share one edge. Either take the panel to 20 px, or bleed it to the card edge so that clearly reads as a different choice. Convention (shared alignment edges), with no catalog entry checked. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- One grid holds the whole page. The logo, headline, subhead and first card all start at x≈56, the right edge of the "Book a visit" button lines up with the right edge of the last card at x≈1224, and the four cards are equal width with even gutters of about 24 px. The page reads as a single built thing.
- The cards line up across columns. Titles (y≈502), descriptions (y≈534) and prices (y≈614) share baselines in all four cards, and the prices sit at the bottom of each card. That makes the prices easy to compare across the row even though "Laundry pickup" and "Window cleaning" have different description lengths.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The band from y≈646 to 800 below the cards is empty. It's probably where the next section starts below the fold, but if the page ends there, that space is leftover rather than planned. Check the full page in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (every element exactly aligned or clearly off).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The hero headline at about x 56–672, y 115–205 breaks as "Help around the house, on your / schedule". The line break splits the phrase "on your schedule", and "schedule" ends up alone on the second line. The reader stalls at "on your", and the word that carries the promise sits by itself as a leftover. The cause is the headline's max-width of about 680 px, which leaves most of the 1280 px width unused. Fix: break after the comma ("Help around the house, / on your schedule"), using a narrower measure, a manual break or `text-wrap: balance`. That makes two balanced lines that each read as a phrase. Convention (good line breaking in display type). Weight: minor. The headline still reads, but it is the first text anyone sees, so the bad break is the most visible flaw in the text.

**What's working.** 
- **The two-face plan is clean.** A bold serif is used only for the wordmark and the headline, and a plain sans carries everything else. The faces are clearly different and each has one job, so nothing looks like a near-miss pairing.
- **The card text uses a few steps that are easy to tell apart.** Each card has a bold title of about 19 px, a grey description of about 15 px and a green bold price of about 15 px. Weight and colour separate the levels instead of extra sizes, so the price is easy to find without adding a fourth size.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The headline wrap depends on viewport width. Check that it breaks at a phrase boundary at the common breakpoints too.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries), 0 unsure

I couldn't run the skill's scripts because Bash was denied. The image is 1280×800, which the guide treats as one screen, so I worked from the whole image without crops. I also couldn't open the reference entries with the entries script, so the finding above cites no specific source. Sizes are estimates by eye, not measured.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The palette is tightly limited.** The interface uses one warm-neutral range (cream ground at about y 68–800, white cards, gray body text) and one hue family: the dark slate of the logo, headline and "Book a visit" button, plus the teal of the prices. The coral, orange, yellow and pale blue appear only inside the four illustration tiles (about y 293–473). Every tile repeats them, so they read as one illustration style and not as scattered extra colors. Keep the brighter hues inside the illustrations.
- **Lightness carries the structure.** The darkest marks on the page are the headline (about 56–672, 115–200), the card titles and the "Book a visit" button (1103–1224, 12–55). Everything else is light, so in grayscale the order still reads: name, headline, services, booking. The saturated colors stay in small areas, so they never compete with the button. Keep the button the only solid dark block in the interface.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There are four flat vector spot illustrations in the service cards (window, bucket, t-shirt, plant pot) and a wordmark logo.

**Findings**
1. **Do the icons and line drawings share one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius?** No. The window cleaning picture (card 1, about x 85–300, y 315–447) is drawn mostly in thick dark navy outline. The frame stroke looks about 6 px, and the squeegee handle is a heavy dark bar. The other three pictures are built from filled shapes and use the dark stroke only once, thinner: the bucket handle (about x 440–545, y 350–385), the t-shirt collar, and the plant stem all look about 3–4 px. The bucket card also adds outlined teal rings, about 2–3 px (x 395–590, y 330–400), as decoration. Only that card has them; the other cards use filled dots and four-point stars. What the viewer sees: the first card looks darker and heavier than the other three, so a row of four equal options gets a slight pull to the left. The pictures also read as close relatives rather than one drawn set. This is minor here because all four share one flat style, one palette and one mint panel, so the set still holds together. Why: this is common sense, since the catalog entry for this line has no approved source. Strokes in a set should share one weight, or differ by a rule, so no single item looks heavier than its peers. Fix: pick one stroke weight for the dark line work and apply it to all four. Either thin the window frame to match the bucket handle, or give the other objects the same outline. Also use one decoration vocabulary across the cards: rings everywhere or nowhere. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- All four pictures share one flat vector style, one muted palette (teal, coral, mustard, navy) and the same pale mint panel at the same size. They read as one family and tie into the brand's teal price links and navy button.
- Each subject is a single clear object, centred in its panel with room around it, and stands well clear of the pale ground. You can tell window, bucket, shirt and plant apart at a glance, even at thumbnail size.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** I could only check the full screenshot (1280×800 px). The crop script couldn't run here because Bash was denied. So stroke widths are eyeballed, and I couldn't check fine edge sharpness at 1:1. Check the pictures zoomed in on a 2× display to confirm they are SVG or high-resolution assets.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius across the drawings)

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes, Interface).** First read: the eye lands on the serif headline, moves down to the four illustrated cards, then up to "Book a visit". It reads as the home page of a local home-services business, calm and friendly but templated. Assumed job: get a homeowner to choose a service and book it. The image is 1280×800, one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

1 primary yes · 2 controls look like what they do **no**: cards at y 280–646 have no signifier, and the teal prices look like links · 3 non-text contrast yes · 4 states yes, none shown · 5 focus unsure · 6 focus obscured unsure · 7 content uncovered yes · 8 targets yes · 9 phone yes, not applicable · 10 status yes · 11 way out yes · 12 inputs yes · 13 destructive yes · 14 recognition yes · 15 disclosure yes · 16–21 forms yes, none shown · 22 empty yes · 23 help yes · 24 shortcuts yes · 25 next action **no**: no ask after the cards, and empty space at y 650–800 · 26 conventions yes · 27 audience words yes · 28 link purpose yes · 29 sensory yes · 30 conceptual model yes · 31 consistency yes · 32 reflow yes · 33 dark patterns yes.

I couldn't open the entries for step 5: Bash was denied, so `entries.mjs` didn't run. The two findings use my own reading and the sources critic.md approves.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies. There is a nav bar, one button, and service cards that may or may not be clickable.

**Findings**
1. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** Where: the four service cards (x 56–1224, y 280–646), and the teal bold "From $89 / $189 / $24 / $65" lines at y ≈ 614.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The subhead tells them to "Pick a service", so they look for a way to pick one. But no card shows that it can be clicked. There's no "Book" or "See details" label, no arrow and no button. Each card is a white panel on a cream page with a faint shadow, which looks the same as a static content box. The teal bold prices are the only thing that looks like a link, and colour is all that marks them. A visitor will either click a price and find out by trial, or decide the cards are just information.
   - **Why:** Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, says a control needs a signifier. Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*, says clickable things must look clickable. A link marked by colour alone also misses WCAG 1.4.1.
   - **Fix:** Decide whether each card is a control. If it is, give it a visible signifier: a text action naming the service, such as "Book window cleaning →", or a secondary-style button at the price line, plus a hover state. If it isn't, take the link colour off the prices so they stop promising a click.
   - Defect, major.
2. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** Where: the hero (y 110–240) and the empty band under the cards (y 650–800).
   - **What the viewer meets:** The subhead lays out a sequence: pick a service, choose a day, a crew arrives. The screen offers neither step where the viewer is reading. The only way to book is the small "Book a visit" button in the top-right corner (x 1103–1224, y 12–55), about 600 px from the cards where the decision gets made. Nothing on the page says whether "Book a visit" carries the chosen service with it or starts over. After reading a card the viewer hits 150 px of empty cream with no next step, so they have to travel back to the header.
   - **Why:** Tognazzini's anticipation principle, an off-list source, so this is my judgment. Krug's point about not making people hunt also applies.
   - **Fix:** Put the next step where the decision happens. Either give each card its own booking action, which also fixes finding 1, or add one primary ask under the hero or the cards that starts the "choose a day" step. Keep the header button as the persistent route.
   - Defect, major.

**What's working.**
- "Book a visit" is the only filled, high-contrast control on the page, and its words name a specific act rather than "Get started". The primary action is clear and spoken in the customer's words.
- The nav has four plain items (Services, Pricing, Service areas, Contact) in the place people expect, with the logo on the left. A first-time visitor can find their way at a glance.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the cards or prices are actually clickable, and their hover states. This decides whether finding 1 is "add a signifier" or "remove the false one".
- The focus indicator on the nav links and the button, and whether a sticky header would cover focused cards.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (every control looks like what it does; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
